prompt: Some schools have replaced letter grades with written feedback only. Write an essay arguing whether this is a good idea.
text:
# Why Schools Should Replace Letter Grades with Written Feedback

A letter grade is a very small message. A "B+" tells a student that the work was good but not excellent. It does not say what was good, what fell short, or what to do next. Written feedback can say all of that. For this reason, I think schools are right to move toward written feedback, as long as they handle three practical problems along the way.

## What a grade does to a student's attention

When students get work back with a grade and a comment, most look at the grade and skip the comment. The grade answers the question they care about most, which is how they did compared with others. Once they have that answer, the comment feels optional.

Research points the same way. In a well-known 1988 study by Ruth Butler, students who received only comments improved more on later tasks than students who received grades, or grades with comments. The grade seemed to pull attention away from the task and toward the student's own standing. Students who got high grades often stopped trying to improve, and students who got low grades often decided they were not good at the subject.

Written feedback avoids this. If the only thing on the page is a comment such as "Your argument is clear, but the second paragraph needs evidence," the student has nothing to read except advice.

## Feedback shows what the student can do

A grade averages many things into one symbol. Two students can both earn a C for different reasons: one writes well but never finishes homework, and the other turns everything in but struggles with the ideas. The letter hides this difference. A written note can describe each student's actual strengths and gaps, which helps teachers, parents and students decide where to spend time.

Written feedback also changes how a mistake feels. A low grade is a verdict. A comment saying "You've got the method right but made an arithmetic slip in step three" is information, and it treats the error as something fixable. Students who see mistakes this way are more willing to attempt hard work.

## The problems are real

Critics raise three objections, and each deserves a straight answer.

**Teacher workload.** Writing thoughtful comments for 150 students takes far more time than assigning letters. If schools adopt written feedback without reducing class sizes or grading loads, the comments will turn into stock phrases like "Good effort, keep it up," which are worse than a grade because they pretend to say something. Schools that make this change need to give teachers the time to do it properly, or they should ask for fewer, better comments on the most important assignments.

**Consistency.** Letters, for all their faults, are fairly easy to compare. Written comments vary with the teacher's style and mood, and a warm teacher may describe the same work more generously than a strict one. Schools can reduce this by agreeing on shared criteria, such as a short list of skills each assignment should show, and by having teachers review samples of each other's comments.

**Colleges and employers.** Universities still expect grade point averages, and a student with only narrative reports may be at a disadvantage if admissions offices cannot read them quickly. Some schools handle this by writing a summary transcript at graduation. Others have found that colleges accept narrative records once they understand them. This problem is a good reason to be careful about timing, but it is not a good reason to keep grades in the early years, when the harm from grading is greatest and the college pressure is far away.

## Where I would draw the line

I would not apply the change evenly across all ages. In elementary and middle school, written feedback should be the default, since students there are still forming their view of themselves as learners. In the final years of high school, a school can reasonably add a summary grade, because students need a record that outside readers can use. Even then, the grade should come after the comments, not instead of them.

## Conclusion

The case for written feedback is that it gives students what they need to improve: specific, honest information about their work, delivered without the verdict that causes many of them to stop reading. The costs are in teacher time, consistency and outside recognition, and all three can be managed with planning and support. A school that drops letter grades without addressing them will do the job badly. A school that addresses them will give students more useful guidance than a letter ever could.
